## What this chapter does

Use this chapter when you are ready to work on the **public Info-Hub website**.

It covers the final publication pathway:

```text
Edit locally
    -> preview and render locally
    -> review the changes
    -> commit and push a branch
    -> merge the branch into main
    -> GitHub Actions renders the site
    -> GitHub Pages publishes the site
    -> check the live website
```

If the change includes new analytical results, complete the appropriate Stata **review, approval and publication** steps first. Quarto should work only with approved public products or their website mirrors.

## Public repository policy

The BNR `info-hub` GitHub repository is **public by design**.

This supports transparent methods, public access to approved outputs and straightforward technical handover.

Public visibility does **not** allow an unauthorised person to change the BNR repository directly. Anyone can read or clone a public repository, and an outside user can make their own fork and propose a pull request. They cannot push changes into `UWI-BNR/info-hub` unless BNR has explicitly granted them suitable repository access.

The practical policy is therefore:

- public code, manuals, Quarto source and approved public products may be committed to `info-hub`;
- confidential data, credentials, REDCap tokens, private review files and private staging material must never be committed;
- only authorised BNR contributors should have write access; and
- routine work should be completed on a branch and merged into `main` only when ready for publication.

`main` is the publication branch. A push or merge to `main` starts the GitHub Pages publication workflow.

## Before you start

Confirm that:

- the workstation has been configured using [Set up a workstation](../getting-started/workstation-setup.qmd);
- any analytical package needed by the page has already been approved and published by Stata;
- you know what website content you intend to change; and
- you are not about to copy a private file into the public repository.

## Step 1: Start a normal Info-Hub editing session

At the root of the local `info-hub` repository, double-click:

`start-info-hub-edit.bat`

The launcher should:

1. check that the repository, Quarto site and Python environment are present;
2. open the repository in VS Code;
3. open a Command Prompt running the Quarto preview server; and
4. open the local Info-Hub in a browser at `http://127.0.0.1:4200/`.

Keep the **BNR info-hub Quarto Preview** command window open while editing. Closing that window stops the local preview server.

The launcher is a convenience only. It does not commit, push or publish anything.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Manual alternative to the launcher

From PowerShell at the repository root:

```powershell
.\venv-info-hub\Scripts\Activate.ps1
cd site
quarto preview --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4200
```

Open the repository separately in VS Code:

```powershell
code ..
```

Stop the preview server with `Ctrl + C`.
:::

## Step 2: Make sure your local copy is up to date

Before starting a new change, update your local `main` branch.

In VS Code:

1. Look at the branch name in the lower-left status bar.
2. If necessary, click the branch name and switch to `main`.
3. Open **Source Control** using the branch icon on the left-hand activity bar.
4. Use the `...` menu and choose **Pull**.
5. Wait for the pull to complete before starting the new branch.

Then create a short working branch:

1. Click the branch name in the lower-left status bar.
2. Choose **Create new branch**.
3. Give it a short descriptive name, for example `update-cvd-briefing` or `publish-cvd-2024-02`.

Do not do routine editing directly on `main`.

Chapter 12 gives more detail on branches and safe code changes. For routine website publication, the steps above are enough.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Git and GitHub in plain English

**Repository**  
The project files and their saved history.

**Local copy / clone**  
The copy of the repository on your workstation.

**Branch**  
A separate working line where you can make and check a change without immediately changing `main`.

**Commit**  
A named checkpoint containing the files you chose to save to Git history.

**Push**  
Send your local commits to GitHub.

**Pull request**  
A GitHub page showing the proposed changes before they are merged into `main`.

**Merge**  
Accept the branch changes into `main`.

**GitHub Actions**  
The automated job that renders and deploys the Info-Hub after `main` changes.

**GitHub Pages**  
The service that hosts the finished public website.
:::

## Step 3: Edit and preview the website

Make the required QMD or website-source changes in VS Code.

Save the file. Quarto preview should normally update the local browser automatically.

Review the changed page while you work. Check:

- headings and text;
- tables and figures;
- links;
- downloads;
- navigation; and
- whether the page remains understandable on a normal browser window.

For general content changes, see [Update website content](update-content.qmd).

## Step 4: Run a complete local render

Preview is useful while editing. Before committing, run a complete render.

Open a **new PowerShell terminal** in VS Code from **Terminal > New Terminal**.

From the repository root:

```powershell
.\venv-info-hub\Scripts\Activate.ps1
cd site
quarto render
```

The render automatically runs the Downloads catalogue builder before Quarto builds the site.

A successful render creates or refreshes:

`site/_site/`

`site/_site/` is generated output and should not be committed to Git.

## Step 5: Review the rendered result

Before committing, inspect the local site.

At minimum:

- open every page you changed;
- follow any new or changed links;
- open new download files;
- check navigation if `_quarto.yml` changed;
- check the Downloads page if an analytical package was published; and
- check that no page points to private staging or another private path.

If something is wrong, fix it locally and render again.

## Step 6: Check exactly what Git will record

Open **Source Control** in VS Code.

The **Changes** list shows files that differ from the last commit.

1. Read the list before staging anything.
2. Click each important file to see the before/after comparison.
3. Confirm that every changed file belongs to the task you intended to complete.
4. Check especially for accidental local configuration, private files or credentials.

Do not commit a file simply because VS Code says it changed.

Typical legitimate website changes include:

- QMD files;
- approved website-mirror files created by the controlled publication workflow;
- `downloads.yml` generated from approved download records;
- site configuration; and
- approved public images or other assets.

## Step 7: Commit and push using VS Code

In the Source Control panel:

1. Click the `+` beside each intended file, or use **Stage All Changes** when the complete Changes list is correct.
2. Enter a short commit message describing the change.
3. Click **Commit**.
4. Click **Publish Branch**, **Push** or **Sync Changes**, depending on what VS Code shows.

After the push, the branch exists on GitHub. The live website has **not** changed yet because the branch has not been merged into `main`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Equivalent basic Git commands

The same routine can be performed in a terminal:

```powershell
git status
git diff
git add <files>
git commit -m "Describe the change"
git push -u origin <branch-name>
```

For routine work, the VS Code Source Control panel is the preferred interface for the BNR team.
:::

## Step 8: Create and merge a pull request on GitHub

Open the [BNR Info-Hub repository](https://github.com/UWI-BNR/info-hub){target="_blank"} in a browser.

1. Open **Pull requests**.
2. Click **New pull request**.
3. Set the **base** branch to `main`.
4. Set the **compare** branch to your working branch.
5. Check the list of changed files.
6. Create the pull request with a short description of the change.
7. Complete any team review required for that change.
8. When the change is ready, choose **Merge pull request** and confirm the merge.

The merge changes `main`. That starts the automated website publication workflow.

After merging, the working branch can normally be deleted from GitHub.

## Step 9: Check GitHub Actions

The repository contains:

`.github/workflows/publish-site.yml`

After `main` changes, GitHub Actions automatically:

1. checks out the repository;
2. installs Quarto;
3. installs Python 3.13;
4. installs the packages in `requirements.txt`;
5. renders the Quarto site from `site/`;
6. uploads `site/_site` as the GitHub Pages website; and
7. deploys it.

To check the run:

1. Open the repository on GitHub.
2. Click **Actions**.
3. Open the newest **Publish Quarto site** run.
4. Confirm that both **build** and **deploy** completed successfully.

A green completed run means GitHub finished its publication job. Still check the live website yourself.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## If GitHub Actions fails

Open the failed run and click the red **build** or **deploy** job.

Open the failed step and read the final error messages.

Common causes include:

- a file used locally was never committed;
- a Python dependency is missing from `requirements.txt`;
- a QMD link or include path is wrong;
- a generated public file expected by the site is absent; or
- `_quarto.yml` contains a formatting error.

Fix the underlying source problem on a branch, render locally again, then commit and merge the correction.

Do not edit the generated GitHub Pages output directly.
:::

## Step 10: Check the live website

After GitHub Actions completes, open the public Info-Hub:

[https://uwi-bnr.github.io/info-hub/](https://uwi-bnr.github.io/info-hub/){target="_blank"}

Check the pages affected by the change.

For an analytical release also check:

- the relevant public dashboard, table or briefing page;
- the expected download link;
- the Downloads catalogue entry; and
- any Latest Data or other listing affected by the release.

Only after this check is the website publication task complete.

## End the editing session

When finished:

1. stop the Quarto preview window with `Ctrl + C` or close the preview Command Prompt;
2. check VS Code Source Control for any unintended uncommitted changes; and
3. close the browser and VS Code when no further work is required.
